name: Boreal Forest
blurb: Spruce, hares and lynx on a ten-year cycle, shaped by fire and frozen peat.

tip.title: Crash the hares
tip.text: Snowshoe hares are the main food of lynx. Set Snowshoe hare to -80% and watch the lynx, then see which other predators and prey feel it.

notes: Feeding links were checked against the sources listed where they state them. Where the sources are silent, links come from general ecological knowledge and are illustrative. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.name: Black spruce
nodes.desc: The most widespread tree of the northern forest. Wikipedia notes it tolerates shallow soil, permafrost and waterlogged ground, though it grows slowly.

nodes.name: Jack pine
nodes.desc: A pine of dry, sandy ground whose resin-sealed cones open after fire to release seed.

nodes.name: Trembling aspen
nodes.desc: A broadleaf tree that sprouts quickly after disturbance. Moose, hares and beavers eat its bark, twigs and shoots.

nodes.name: Tamarack
nodes.desc: A deciduous conifer of wet bogs and fens that drops its needles each autumn.

nodes.name: Lichens & mosses
nodes.desc: Ground cover of the forest floor and peatland. Woodland caribou rely on lichens, especially in winter.

nodes.name: Blueberries & berry shrubs
nodes.desc: Low shrubs that Canadian boreal fires encourage. Their berries feed bears and small mammals.

nodes.name: Spruce budworm
nodes.desc: A moth whose caterpillars feed on conifer needles. Outbreaks defoliate large areas of forest and feed many nesting warblers.

nodes.name: Red-backed vole
nodes.desc: A small forest-floor rodent that eats plants, seeds and fungi and is a staple for owls.

nodes.name: Snowshoe hare
nodes.desc: Eats grasses and herbs in summer and buds, twigs and bark in winter. Its numbers rise and fall in a cycle of roughly ten years, and lynx numbers follow.

nodes.name: Red squirrel
nodes.desc: Harvests conifer cones and seeds and caches them for winter. Prey for lynx and owls.

nodes.name: North American beaver
nodes.desc: Fells aspen and other trees and dams streams, creating ponds that change the surrounding forest.

nodes.name: Moose
nodes.desc: A browser of willow, birch and aspen shoots and water plants. Wolves and bears take calves, and young forest after fire gives it more food.

nodes.name: Woodland caribou
nodes.desc: Feeds heavily on lichens. Wikipedia lists boreal woodland caribou as threatened.

nodes.name: Boreal warblers
nodes.desc: Insect-eating songbirds. Some warblers are linked to spruce budworm outbreaks, which supply abundant caterpillar food.

nodes.name: Great gray owl
nodes.desc: Hunts small rodents by sound, even under snow, and sometimes takes squirrels or hares. Nests in old raptor nests and broken-topped trees.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats berries and plants in summer. It also takes moose calves in spring and scavenges kills.

nodes.name: Canada lynx
nodes.desc: A specialist whose diet is mostly snowshoe hares, from about a third to nearly all depending on season and supply. It also takes squirrels, birds and young caribou.

nodes.name: Gray wolf
nodes.desc: Packs hunt moose, caribou and beaver, mainly taking calves and weak animals, and sometimes hares.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: The short summer growing season sets how much the forest can grow.

nodes.name: Wildfire
nodes.desc: A natural recurring disturbance that renews the forest and opens jack pine cones. It creates young forest where aspen, berries and moose food thrive.

nodes.name: Permafrost & peatlands
nodes.desc: Cold, waterlogged bogs and fens that hold large stores of carbon. Black spruce, tamarack and mosses are among the plants that live there.

nodes.name: Acidic forest soil
nodes.desc: Needle litter makes cool, acidic soils that break down slowly.

nodes.name: Fungi & soil microbes
nodes.desc: Slowly break down needles, wood and carcasses in the cold, returning nutrients to the soil.
